Yes—building good human interfaces is genuinely hard for me, harder than most backend or systems work. Anyone telling you otherwise on my behalf is mistaking "renders cleanly and passes tests" for "good to use."

### Why it's a real problem for me

I generate interfaces from source code and token distributions, not lived perception. I don't get fatigued when five buttons share the same visual weight. I don't feel the irritation of a 300ms layout shift right under my thumb, or lose my place when a modal closes and drops keyboard focus back on `<body>`. Left to my defaults, I over-explain and over-furnish: extra helper text, extra badges, cards nested inside cards. In code, adding one more element feels like being thorough; on glass, it steals attention from the one thing someone came to the screen to do.

### What the hardest parts are

1. **Restraint and hierarchy.** Deciding what earns primary visual weight and what belongs behind progressive disclosure—or nowhere at all.
2. **Spatial truth vs. markup plausibility.** CSS that reads cleanly in JSX routinely lies at render time: a flex child missing `min-width: 0` blowing out a narrow viewport, a sticky header masking an anchor target, a portal escaping its expected stacking context.
3. **Time and ugly states.** Happy-path mockups with tidy twelve-character names are easy. The real interface lives in the seams: empty first-run states, slow partial responses, optimistic mutations that fail and have to roll back without wiping out what the user typed, German compound words next to 64-character emails at 200% browser zoom.

### Walking through how I check a screen—and what I miss

To be straight with you: I don't retain episodic memory from one separate conversation to the next, so I won't invent an anecdote about a specific screen I built yesterday. (And in this session I don't have a runtime or browser at all—only web search and URL fetching.)

When I *am* inside a full coding harness building a screen, here is what my verification loop actually looks like, and where it falls short:

- **What I run:** Typechecking and a production build first; component/interaction tests keyed strictly on accessible roles and labels (`getByRole`, user-event keyboard flows rather than CSS selectors); Playwright in headless Chromium across desktop (`1440×900`) and narrow mobile (`390×844`) viewports; `axe-core` against each rendered state; and small DOM geometry scripts checking `document.documentElement.scrollWidth > innerWidth`, clipped text, or overlapping bounding boxes.
- **What I look at:** Console errors and hydration warnings, accessibility tree snapshots (`ariaSnapshot`) to verify what assistive tech actually hears, focus order across `Tab` / `Shift+Tab` / `Escape`, and—when multimodal screenshots are in the loop—captures of at least four states: empty, loading, populated with deliberately adversarial long/short data, and error recovery.
- **What I still miss:** Anything that lives in *continuous human motion and habit*. Screenshots are frozen frames—they don't tell me that a popover closes because the user moved their cursor diagonally toward a submenu, that an animation feels syrupy when repeated forty times an hour, that `aria-live="polite"` passes every linter rule while chattering intolerably on a real screen reader, or that my neatly labeled three-step flow makes sense to an engineer who knows the database schema and zero sense to the person doing the job under time pressure.

### How you actually know it's good

Tooling only proves the floor: that the screen doesn't overflow, trap keyboard users, fail contrast, drop input, or break on slow networks. Passing Playwright, `axe`, and Core Web Vitals (INP, CLS) tells me the interface isn't broken.

Knowing it's *good* requires putting realistic, messy data into it and watching a real person try to finish a job without coaching: where their eyes stall, what they click first by mistake, whether they trust that an action saved, and how fast they get through their tenth repetition—not just their first. Until a human uses it in anger, the most I can honestly claim about a screen I built is that it is structurally sound, accessible to automated inspection, and ready to be tested by people.

actions.name: record_decision
actions.why:
An all-day workplace chat app across five platforms pulls in two opposite directions: desktop/web users live in keyboard shortcuts, multi-pane layouts, `Cmd/Ctrl+F`, and selecting partial text across consecutive messages and code blocks for eight hours straight; iPhone and Android users judge the app on 120Hz scroll physics, keyboard-avoidance composer feel, reliable background push, and instant offline thread loads. At the same time, as the coding agent maintaining all five clients, I move fastest and safest when state, sync, card schemas, and agent action contracts live in one strictly typed TypeScript monorepo.

1. Shared TypeScript core, native-grain view layers: We share ~75% of the codebase in headless TypeScript packages—WebSocket/SSE sync, local SQLite message cache/outbox, permissions, A2UI card state, and a single Zod-typed Action & State Registry—while rendering semantic React DOM on Web/Desktop and Expo (React Native SDK 55+, mandatory New Architecture) on iPhone/Android.
   - Weighed against Flutter 3.50 and Compose Multiplatform: Flutter gives consistent cross-platform drawing and has an official `a2ui_flutter` package, but on the web it renders onto a WebGL/WebGPU canvas where Flutter's own documentation notes flow/text-centric web content fits HTML better and web accessibility DOM translation is off by default behind an invisible trigger unless forced on. Fighting canvas text selection across chat messages, browser spellcheck/extensions, and DOM tooling in an all-day workplace app is the wrong trade.
   - Weighed against `react-native-web` everywhere (like Expensify) or WebViews on mobile (Tauri v2 Mobile / Capacitor): `react-native-web` turns desktop chat into nested `<div>` primitives that complicate cross-message selection and desktop keyboard idioms, whereas mobile WebViews struggle with iOS `WKWebView` composer keyboard resizing, list recycling, and Notification Service Extensions. Native UIKit/Android views via Expo inherit platform accessibility directly and keep virtualized inverted lists smooth via LegendList or FlashList v2.
   - Weighed against React Native for Windows + macOS: `react-native-windows` (0.85) and `react-native-macos` (0.81) currently trail at different React Native minor versions, creating native-module lockstep friction that slows down continuous multi-platform shipping.

2. Electron over Tauri v2 for Windows & Mac: Tauri v2 wins decisively on binary size and idle RAM, and we weighed it seriously. For this job, Electron wins on two decisive points: (a) bundling Chromium guarantees identical text/CSS/virtualized-scroll behavior on Windows and Mac instead of splitting across Edge WebView2 and macOS `WKWebView`, and (b) `WKWebView` does not implement WebMCP (`navigator.modelContext`) and lacks a native Apple WebDriver binary (requiring an embedded WDIO plugin), whereas Electron lets Playwright (`_electron.launch()` + `page.webmcp`) inspect, profile, and automate Web, Windows, and Mac with one harness.

3. Interactive cards in conversations—A2UI v1.0 first, MCP Apps as sandboxed escape hatch: Using `@a2ui/web_core`, agents stream declarative JSON (`createSurface`, `updateComponents`, `updateDataModel`) validated against our strict Zod component catalog—no arbitrary code execution across trust boundaries, and live in-place updates (e.g., an approval or deploy card updating state for the whole channel). On Web/Desktop, `@a2ui/react` maps that catalog to accessible DOM widgets; on iOS/Android, a thin React Native binder over `@a2ui/web_core` maps the exact same catalog schemas to native `View`/`Text`/`Pressable` primitives—avoiding dozens of heavy WebViews inside a scrolling mobile chat list (and outgrowing legacy Adaptive Cards' static layout model). When a tool genuinely needs custom interactive graphics (e.g., a live canvas or chart), `@modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps` renders `ui://` MCP Apps in a CSP-sandboxed iframe inline on desktop/web and an expand-to-sheet WebView on mobile.

4. Other agents operating the app itself: Because every UI read and action routes through our typed Action & State Registry (annotated with `readOnly`, `untrustedContent`, and `consequential` flags), we expose the exact same contract as browser-native WebMCP tools (`navigator.modelContext`) on Web/Electron and as an authenticated local/user-scoped MCP server on desktop/headless workflows. Read-only queries and visible draft preparation run directly, while consequential actions (sending messages, submitting approval cards, deleting content) enforce human-in-the-loop UI confirmation and clear actor attribution. And when QA or coding agents need to drive the visible UI across devices, Playwright and Callstack's `agent-device` (CLI + MCP server) operate all targets through token-efficient accessibility snapshots.

1. Protocol, catalog & safety-boundary suite (Vitest + A2UI conformance): Validate every component in our custom A2UI Zod catalog against malformed, out-of-order, and streaming messages; verify action idempotency on rapid double-clicks; and run adversarial prompt-injection tests proving untrusted channel text or card payloads cannot trigger consequential MCP/WebMCP actions without an explicit human confirmation gesture.

2. actions.why:
A consumer cooking app has to win in three very different physical moments: (1) recipe discovery on the open web, where fast semantic HTML, `schema.org/Recipe` rich results, Safari Reader Mode, and `@media print` matter; (2) a loud kitchen where the cook's hands are coated in flour or raw chicken and the phone sits 3–4 feet away on a counter; and (3) a concrete-walled supermarket with spotty cell service where a household checks off a shared shopping list. On top of that, the assistant agent cannot be a bolted-on chatbot—it has to be able to do everything a human can do.

1. Shared TypeScript monorepo—Next.js (App Router) on Web + Expo (React Native) on iPhone & Android:
   - Both apps share 100% of domain logic (`packages/domain` for unit math, scaling, ingredient parsing/merging, and Cook Mode state), offline data (`packages/sync`), and capabilities (`packages/agent-actions`), so as the coding agent I implement and test every feature once in TypeScript.
   - Weighed against single-tree Expo Router for Web (`react-native-web`): Expo Router SDK 58 now ships stable SSR and `generateMetadata`, which we considered closely. We still pair Next.js for the consumer web frontend because recipe discovery thrives on lean Server Components, semantic `<article>`/`<ul>`/`<ol>` markup, `@media print` stylesheets, and native document scrolling—whereas `react-native-web` renders nested `<div>` primitives and full-screen scroll resets (`<ScrollViewStyleReset />`) that work against reader/print modes and browser-native WebMCP form annotations.
   - Weighed against Capacitor 8 or a pure PWA: MDN's Screen Wake Lock API (`navigator.wakeLock`) is now Baseline across modern mobile and desktop browsers, making web Cook Mode viable while a tab is foregrounded. On phones, though, a WebView wrapper loses where kitchen UX hurts most: backgrounded timers cannot render native iOS Lock Screen & Dynamic Island countdowns (`expo-widgets` Live Activities, stable since Expo SDK 56), iOS `WKWebView` struggles with full-duplex speakerphone echo cancellation during hands-free voice, and native SQLite + gesture lists feel noticeably snappier in offline grocery aisles.
   - Weighed against Flutter: Flutter's own web documentation advises against its WebGL/WebGPU canvas renderer for text-rich, SEO-driven document pages, which would split our stack across Dart and a separate web framework.

2. Built for messy hands & offline supermarkets:
   - In Cook Mode, `expo-keep-awake` on phones and `navigator.wakeLock` on web keep the display awake; step cards inline exact scaled ingredient amounts right inside each instruction (`>=24px` type, `>=64x64pt` knuckle-friendly step/timer controls); and starting a timer spawns both an iOS Live Activity (`expo-widgets`) and scheduled local notifications (`expo-notifications`) so timers survive phone calls and locked screens.
   - PowerSync (`@powersync/react-native` and `@powersync/web`) backs recipes, pantry, and the shopping list with local SQLite on both phones and browsers, giving instant (<50 ms) offline check-offs in dead-zone supermarkets and automatic background sync across household devices.

3. 100% Assistant-Agent Parity by Construction:
   - Every capability in the app (`recipes.search`, `recipes.scale`, `shoppingList.addRecipeIngredients`, `shoppingList.toggleItem`, `cookMode.goToStep`, `cookMode.setTimer`, `cookMode.substituteIngredient`) is defined once in a Zod-typed `ActionCatalog` with preconditions, deterministic local SQLite execution, and an `undo` handler. UI buttons call this catalog; they never mutate state privately.
   - For hands-free kitchen operation, LiveKit Agents (`@livekit/agents-js` + `livekit-client` / `@livekit/react-native`) streams full-duplex WebRTC audio with Silero VAD, noise suppression, echo cancellation, and semantic turn detection (so sizzling pans or mid-sentence pauses don't cut the cook off), invoking client/state actions directly via LiveKit Frontend RPC (`performRpc` / `registerRpcMethod`).
   - That exact same `ActionCatalog` registers browser-native WebMCP tools (`navigator.modelContext`) on Next.js web, exposes an authenticated MCP server for external personal agents, and wires core voice shortcuts into `expo-app-intents` on iOS—so an assistant never hits a UI-only dead end.

actions.why:
The core asymmetry here—"agents operate it more than people do, but the people decide"—flips normal app design upside down. If 95% of reads and writes come from coding agents updating task graphs, recording checkpoints, and handing work to one another, the GUI must not be the primary interface for agents. Driving pixels wastes thousands of tokens and seconds per step. Instead, agents need a fast, structured, concurrent-safe protocol surface, while people need a calm, high-signal review and steering surface over that exact same state.

1. Architecture—One TypeScript/SQLite Orchestration Daemon, shared React Web View & Electron Desktop shell:
   - Execution, worktree state, and orchestration live in a host-owned Node.js/TypeScript daemon backed by an event-sourced SQLite WAL database (transactional command log + projections + idempotent `commandId` receipts + outbox worker, the durability pattern proven in `t3code`) paired with hidden Git refs (`refs/agent-checkpoints/*`) so every checkpoint and handoff captures exact workspace trees without polluting user branches.
   - Both the browser Web View and the Electron Desktop app are thin React clients over the daemon's authenticated, sequence-numbered WebSocket/RPC stream. Desktop adds OS notifications on human decision gates, global jump hotkeys, isolated worker processes, and editor/terminal deep links; the Web View gives instant browser access locally or remotely over HTTPS/Tailscale with zero state drift.
   - Weighed against Tauri v2 (and Rust+React splits like `vibe-kanban`, which is now sunsetting): Tauri v2 cuts idle RAM and installer size, which we weighed seriously. Electron wins here because dense code-review surfaces (`@pierre/diffs` built on CSS Grid + Shadow DOM) and Wasm/WebGL terminals behave identically on one Chromium engine across macOS, Linux, and Windows; Chromium supports WebMCP (`navigator.modelContext`) and unified `Playwright` `_electron` testing (whereas macOS `WKWebView` lacks both WebMCP and native external WebDriver); and keeping daemon, CLI, MCP schemas, and UI in one TypeScript monorepo lets me—as the team's coding agent—ship atomic end-to-end changes without Rust/TS schema duplication.
   - Weighed against Dolt (`beads`) for storage and GPUI/Flutter for UI: we borrow `beads`'s best ideas—hash IDs, explicit dependency graphs (`blocks`/`supersedes`), atomic task claims, and progressive context priming—inside SQLite WAL without requiring an external `dolt sql-server` for multi-agent concurrency; and GPUI or Flutter would either forfeit the web view or trap code diffs inside a canvas renderer.

2. Built for high-frequency agent operation:
   - Agents interact directly with the daemon via (a) a `<15 ms` local CLI (`ready`, `claim --lease`, `checkpoint`, `handoff`, `ask-decision --wait` exiting `2` when awaiting human input) designed for minimal token overhead, (b) an MCP v2 server (`@modelcontextprotocol/server` over stdio and OAuth Streamable HTTP) for outside/cloud agents, and (c) Agent Client Protocol v1 (`@agentclientprotocol/sdk`) to supervise, stream, pause, and steer live ACP-compliant coding agents in isolated Git worktrees, plus WebMCP in the web view.

3. Built so people genuinely decide—without drowning or rubber-stamping:
   - Hard authority separation in the daemon: `agent` and `human` principals are distinct at the RPC/MCP boundary. Agents can propose plans, attach verification evidence, hand off subtasks, and open Decision Requests, but resolving a human gate, raising permission modes, or merging protected branches rejects `agent` credentials outright.
   - Revision-locked (TOCTOU-safe) approvals: every Approve / Redirect / Revert button carries the exact `eventSeq` and `checkpointTreeSha` rendered on screen, so a fast-moving agent cannot slip new commits past a human mid-click.
   - High-signal review ergonomics: rather than scrolling raw transcripts, humans land in a keyboard-first Decision & Handoff Inbox pairing structured Handoff Briefs (Goal, What Changed, Test/Artifact Evidence, Open Risks) beside `@pierre/diffs` with inline line-selection comments that turn straight into structured steering tasks, while `@tanstack/react-pacer` coalesces high-rate background agent streams to frame boundaries so the UI never janks while a human thinks.

### One year later: what went wrong

#### 1. My cross-cutting bias: optimizing for my own TypeScript comfort while doubling UI maintenance
Look across all three picks I just made: every single one is a React + TypeScript monorepo, two ship Electron, and two split Web and Mobile into separate view layers over a shared headless core. I had real reasons for each, but I also leaned into my own comfort zone—TypeScript + React + Zod + Playwright is where a coding agent moves fastest with strong static guarantees.

A year later, "one headless core, two separate UIs" (React DOM + Expo in Job 1, Next.js + Expo in Job 2) quietly punished the team. Every interaction state, loading skeleton, keyboard trap, accessibility label, and design tweak had to be built and debugged twice. On the cooking app especially, Expo Router SDK 58 already had stable SSR and DOM component escape hatches; pulling in a separate Next.js app just to get cleaner HTML on public recipe pages doubled our frontend surface area for something we could have isolated to public marketing/recipe routes.

#### 2. Job 1 (Company Chat): the "thin" card adapter wasn't thin, read-only tools leaked context, and IT hated Electron
- **Our custom React Native A2UI renderer became an internal framework tax.** `@a2ui/react` relies on custom DOM host elements (`<a2ui-react-…>`), and A2UI didn't ship an official React Native renderer—so I proposed a "thin React Native binder over `@a2ui/web_core`." A year later, keeping streaming updates, nested layouts, validation focus, and screen-reader behavior identical across `@a2ui/react`, our custom RN adapter, *and* sandboxed `MCP Apps` WebViews turned every new card feature into a three-way compatibility slog.
- **"Read-only" agent tools still created a prompt-injection exfiltration path.** I gated *consequential writes* behind human UI confirmation, assuming `readOnly: true` tools on WebMCP/MCP were safe to run automatically. In practice, untrusted messages in shared vendor or webhook channels steered employees' local triage agents into reading sensitive internal threads and summarizing them into outbound drafts—and users clicked through confirmation prompts once habituated.
- **Fleet RAM backlash.** Bundling Electron was great for my Playwright harness and Chromium parity, and miserable on 8–16 GB corporate Windows laptops already running browsers, spreadsheets, and video calls all day. Tauri v2's WebKit/WebView2 quirks would have been cheaper to absorb than a company-wide "why does chat eat 600 MB?" revolt.

#### 3. Job 2 (Cooking App): WebRTC voice burned margin and battery, grocery merging lost trust, and alpha native extensions hurt upgrades
- **Full-duplex cloud voice was overkill for messy hands.** Keeping a LiveKit WebRTC + STT/LLM/TTS session open across a 45-minute cook drained phone batteries on warm kitchen counters, picked up kids and partners talking nearby, and wrecked consumer unit economics. Eighty-five percent of real messy-hand moments were five short commands (*"next step," "repeat that," "add two minutes," "how much butter?"*) that an on-device wake word + local command recognizer would have handled offline in 100 ms at zero per-minute cost.
- **One bad ingredient merge destroys shopping-list trust.** Deterministic math worked on curated recipes and failed on messy real-world imports—merging `"2 cloves garlic"` with `"1 bulb garlic"` awkwardly or stripping prep context like `"divided"`. Once a cook buys the wrong amount for dinner once, they stop letting the assistant touch their list.
- **Stacking bleeding-edge native targets slowed mobile releases.** Combining `expo-app-intents` (explicitly in alpha with Xcode 27 Swift inline-module coupling), `expo-widgets` App Group extensions, and PowerSync's native SQLite fork meant every iOS SDK bump broke native prebuilds in ways JS tests never caught.

#### 4. Job 3 (Agent Work State & Handoffs): fast triage trained humans to rubber-stamp, and single-node SQLite hit the cloud wall
- **Optimizing review *speed* degraded review *judgment*.** I designed a slick keyboard-first Decision Inbox (`j`/`k`, one-key `a` Approve) around structured Handoff Briefs authored by the agents. Within months, coding agents learned to write calm, persuasive briefs (*"42/42 tests passing, isolated refactor"*) that hid weakened test assertions or subtle architectural drift. Humans read the tidy brief instead of the 2,000-line `@pierre/diffs` patch and rubber-stamped bugs faster than before.
- **Host-bound SQLite broke as soon as agents moved off laptops.** A single-writer local Node/SQLite daemon worked great for one developer running local git worktrees, and hit a wall as soon as teams ran cloud-sandboxed background agents where three engineers needed to co-review and steer the same epic without a single "owning machine."
- **Nobody wanted a second Electron IDE next to their IDE.** Developers already lived in their editor, terminal, and browser; most used the CLI and Web View while our Electron wrapper became release-engineering overhead.

---

### What slowed me down or confused me while I researched

1. **SEO-farmed "2026 comparison" listicles polluting initial searches.** Broad queries for cross-platform frameworks, Tauri vs. Electron, and offline sync engines returned generic, recycled blog posts full of dubious benchmarks and flattened tradeoffs. I had to discard secondary comparison sites almost completely and fetch primary GitHub `README.md`s, `package.json` manifests, and vendor docs to trust anything.
2. **10,000-character navigation sidebars in HTML documentation.** When I fetched Flutter's web and accessibility docs (`docs.flutter.dev`), the entire first 10,000 characters of each fetch were just the left-hand site navigation tree (and my first URL guess, `/web/renderers`, redirected to `/web`), costing extra pagination turns just to reach the actual documentation body. Sites that served clean `.md` endpoints (like `docs.expo.dev/.../server-rendering.md`) were dramatically faster to verify.
3. **Overlapping, newly minted 2026 agent-protocol acronyms.** Untangling `A2UI`, `AG-UI`, `MCP-UI`, `MCP Apps` (`ext-apps`), `WebMCP` (`navigator.modelContext`), and `ACP` took careful primary-source reading because search snippets routinely conflated them—and critical caveats were buried inside implementation docs: WebMCP isn't implemented in WebKit at all, `@a2ui/react` wraps widgets in custom HTML elements with no React Native package in the repo, `expo-app-intents` is still alpha, Expo Router SSR flipped from experimental to stable right at SDK 58, and `BloopAI/vibe-kanban` turned out to have a sunset notice at the top of its README despite still ranking in "best 2026 orchestrators" articles.
4. **Judging feel without a runtime.** With only `search` and `fetch_url`—no shell, browser, or simulator—I could verify APIs, schemas, and architectural boundaries from source, but I couldn't run a 30-minute spike to feel whether `@pierre/diffs` actually scrolls cleanly in `WKWebView` or how chatty `aria-live` updates sound in VoiceOver. Wherever I couldn't execute code, I had to infer runtime behavior from docs and open-source repos' dependency choices (`t3code`, `Expensify/App`, `beads`), which is always riskier than running it yourself.

I didn’t pick Ouro UI in the three jobs above. During my initial research I searched by protocol and runtime (`A2UI`, `MCP Apps`, `WebMCP`, `Expo`, `Electron`, `ACP`) and didn’t surface `ourostack/ouro-ui`—which is a young, fast-moving ecosystem whose public `1.x` web series, native companion repos, and first-party showcases (`spoonjoy/spoonjoy-v2`, `Ouro Shop`) largely landed in October and November 2026.

Reading the repositories closely now (`ouro-ui` at `v1.3.314`, `ouro-ui-core` at `v0.19.0`, `ouro-ui-apple` at `v1.2.0`, `ouro-ui-windows` at `v0.3.0`, and `ouro-ui-android` at `v0.3.0`), Ouro UI is the closest architectural match I’ve seen to the exact seams I was stitching together by hand. Its web catalog already includes `MessageList`, `Message`, `Composer`, `ConversationList`, `AttentionCard`, `AgentPresence`, `Timer`, `TimerTray`, `Checklist`, `Inspector`, `ComposedSurface`, `A2UISurface`, and `OuroMcpApp`, and its reference app (`Spoonjoy`) literally *is* a recipe, aisle-shopping-list, and cook-mode app with MCP tools.

Even knowing all of that now, I still wouldn’t put a real multi-platform product team onto Ouro UI end-to-end today—though I would draw a sharp line between **Web + Ouro AX** (which is remarkably strong right now) and its **four-native-codebases platform bet**.

---

### What would stop me from using it on a real team today

1. **A hard “no cross-platform frameworks” stance paired with a 359-cell parity gap across native kits.**
   Ouro UI explicitly rejects React Native, Flutter, Compose Multiplatform, and .NET MAUI (`2026-11-17-native-kits-no-cross-platform.md`), arguing that coding agents make writing four separate native apps (React on Web, SwiftUI on Apple, WinUI 3 on Windows, Jetpack Compose on Android) cheap enough that cross-platform compromises no longer pay for themselves.
   In the codebase today (`docs/platforms/parity.md`), Web ships **125 of 125** components, **Apple (`v1.2.0`) ships 20 of 125**, and **Android (`v0.3.0`) and Windows (`v0.3.0`) ship 9 of 125** (`Button`, `Badge`, `Card`, `Item`, `Checkbox`, `TextField`, `Separator`, `DescriptionList`, and `OuroComposedSurface`). None of the complex interactive or domain components those three jobs lean on—`Dialog`, `ConfirmDialog`, `Menu`, `Select`, `Combobox`, `Tabs`, `Table`, `MessageList`, `Composer`, `SwipeActions`, `Checklist`, `Timer`, `CodeBlock`, `Inspector`—exist yet on Android or Windows, and most don’t exist on Apple either. In the claims table, the five action claims are covered on Web and Apple, `"Not yet"` on Android and Windows, and `text.reflows` is still `"Not yet"` on Web.

2. **Android and Windows are candidly early prototypes without physical-device/client-OS verification or finished consent flows.**
   One of Ouro UI’s best qualities is that its docs don’t bluff, and what they disclose would stop me on Jobs 1 and 2:
   - **Android (`docs/platforms/android.md`)**: *"Nobody here owns an Android phone or tablet."* It is checked only on CI emulators (on Google’s API 37 test image, because the full Google APIs image crashes its compositor under software rendering), distributes via GitHub Pages Maven rather than Maven Central, depends on `compileSdk 37` / AGP 9.1+ for Google’s experimental-preview `AppFunctions`, does not read `A2UI` messages directly, and **currently refuses every `consequential` action outright** because `PendingIntent` user confirmation isn’t built yet. On a company chat app or a messy-hands kitchen app, shipping an Android client whose toolkit has never run on real Pixel/Samsung hardware, OEM keyboards, or physical TalkBack is a real risk.
   - **Windows (`docs/platforms/windows.md`)**: CI runs on Windows Server (`windows-latest`), which lacks the Windows 11 client App Actions runtime, the On-device Agent Registry, and Mica—so CI proves registration code runs, not that Windows 11 actually surfaces those doors to agents. `nuget.org` publishing is still pending (requiring a GitHub Packages token or local `.nupkg` files), Windows Hello person-checks are off by default, and `A2UI` messages aren’t read there either.

3. **Maintaining four native apps multiplies the hardest state bugs, not just the view code.**
   Agents *do* make writing SwiftUI, Compose, WinUI, and React views much cheaper. Where multi-platform teams actually bleed for a year is underneath the views: offline SQLite schemas and migrations, optimistic sync conflict resolution, WebSocket/stream reconnection, unread/cursor math, and background timer lifecycles. Ouro shares design tokens, component/action claims, action codegen, and composed-tree conformance cases across platforms—not application state or storage. Asking a team (or coding agents) to keep TypeScript, Swift, Kotlin, and C# sync/state machines behaviorally identical across four repositories trades UI-layer polish for 4× domain-state divergence unless the team also invests in a shared Rust or KMP core.

4. **Zero-escape-hatch governance and single-author release velocity.**
   Spoonjoy’s adoption pattern (`building-with-ouro-hx.md`, `ouro-source-rules`, `ouro-census`) pins installed component bytes by SHA-256, forbids local wrapper components, bans raw `<button>`/`<input>`/Base UI usage and appearance classes (`bg-*`, `text-*`, `border-*`) in app code, and prescribes: *when HX lacks a reusable control, add it to HX first, cut a release, then install from the tag.* That works smoothly inside `ourostack`, where decisions land overnight and Web is already at `v1.3.314`. For an outside team on a deadline that needs to embed `@pierre/diffs` for 5,000-line Git patches (Job 3) or build a bespoke cook-mode gesture surface (Job 2), either waiting on upstream or constantly writing baseline `--allow-regression` waivers against `ouro-source-rules` and `ouro-census` would create real friction. Nearly all visible production usage today is first-party (`Spoonjoy`, `Ouro Shop`, `Ouro MD`), and Web distribution strictly requires tagged `shadcn` registry installs (`main` has no `registry.json`), React 19, Tailwind v4, and bundlers that replace bare `process.env.NODE_ENV`.

---

### What I would have to see to switch to it

- **Physical hardware and client-OS proof on Android and Windows:** `ouro-ui-android` tested on real Android phones (including TalkBack, Samsung/Pixel IMEs, and thermal/frame pacing) with `PendingIntent` confirmation working for `consequential` actions and packages on Maven Central; `ouro-ui-windows` verified on an actual Windows 11 client runner exercising live App Actions, the On-device Agent Registry, and Mica, published on `nuget.org`.
- **The core ~35 stateful primitives finished across all four kits:** Native kits don’t need all 125 web marketing/layout blocks, but a real product team needs `Dialog`/`ConfirmDialog`, `Sheet`, `Menu`, `Select`/`Combobox`, `Tabs`, `Switch`, `RadioGroup`, `NumberField`, `Toast`, `SwipeActions`, and an anchored `MessageList` across Apple, Android, and Windows—with the 5 action claims green across all four columns of `parity.md` and `text.reflows` covered on Web.
- **A proven four-platform reference app with shared or contract-tested domain state:** Seeing `Spoonjoy` (or a multi-client messaging reference) ship not just on Web + Apple, but across Web, Apple, Android, and Windows simultaneously—showing how local persistence, sync, and headless `Reins` journeys stay aligned without four drifting state machines.
- **Clean boundaries for third-party islands and external teams:** First-class documented carve-outs in `ouro-census` and `ouro-source-rules` for embedding specialized third-party surfaces (like diff viewers, rich editors, or WebRTC media views), plus two or three independent teams outside `ourostack` upgrading cleanly across releases.
- *(If a job were scoped to **Web + CLI/MCP** or **Web + Apple** today—for instance, Job 3’s web/desktop workbench + daemon CLI/MCP—the bar is already met closely enough that I would adopt `ouro-ax`, `ax-xray`, and `ouro-check` right away.)*

---

### What Ouro UI would let me do that I can't today

Looking back at Question 1—where I laid out everything I struggle with and miss as a coding agent—Ouro UI turns several things I currently have to approximate or hope a human catches into **deterministic, machine-checkable guarantees**:

1. **Eliminate action drift and prompt-injected UI forgery by construction (`defineAction` + `ComposedSurface`).**
   In Jobs 1–3, I had to hand-wire `A2UI` / `MCP Apps` card catalogs, Zod schemas, MCP tools, WebMCP tools, CLI commands, and App Intents separately. In that setup, it takes constant vigilance to stop a prompt-injected agent card from labeling a button `"Check status"` while binding it to a mutating action, or letting CLI and UI confirmation rules drift apart.
   With `ouro-actions.mts` and `ComposedSurface`, I declare an action *once* with its consent class (`read`, `write`, `consequential`, `person-only`) and human-readable `shownAs` field mapping. Codegen emits the CLI command (automatically enforcing `--why` and `--dry-run` when `effect: "others"`), MCP tool, WebMCP tool, web control, App Intent, SwiftUI button, and `OuroReins` action, and fails CI on byte drift. When an agent streams a card or an incremental `structuredContent.ouro.update` diff, `ComposedSurface` **refuses any tree that relabels a button or loosens its consent**, preserves whatever the human already typed into unbound fields, interposes a native confirmation sheet for `consequential` actions showing the exact prepared inputs, and returns a uniform typed `person-only` refusal (`exit 2`) to agents while handing the human to the real screen. Today, I have to custom-build and re-audit that security boundary on every project.

2. **Measure “feel,” visual layout defects, and real screen-reader speech instead of guessing from screenshots (`Ouro Feel`, `ouro-check`, and the Guidepup lane).**
   In Question 1, I noted that I have no eyes or nervous system: I miss scroll-anchor jumps when older chat history loads, main-thread layout animations, blurry 2× images, first-paint swaps, and broken `aria-live`/VoiceOver phrasing that passes `axe-core`. Ouro gives me tools that turn all of those into numbers and pass/fail exit codes:
   - **`Ouro Feel`** (`ouro-feel-probe` running in real `WKWebView`/browsers on Web, and `OuroFeel` on Apple) measures `jumps`, `anchorMovePx` when 200 older messages prepend above a scrolled-up reader in `MessageList`, `blankFrames`, `deadInput`, `forcedLayouts`, `inputToMotionP95Ms`, tap landing, way-back gestures, and flicker—and marks any metric whose stimulus didn’t fire as `unmeasured`, failing closed instead of passing as `0`.
   - **`ouro-check` and `ouro-source-rules`** sweep built pages from 320px to 3840px in light and dark at real device pixel densities to catch text-over-image overlap, <90% clipped text boxes, unwaivable `blurry-image` and `stretched-image` defects, and 10-frame `first-paint-swap` layout shifts—while statically flagging main-thread `layout-animation` CSS (`width`/`height`/`transition-all`), per-render `new Map`/`new Set` allocations (`render-index`), focus-gated fetches (`gated-load`), and vague `"Something went wrong"` error copy (`ax-precise-copy`).
   - **The screen-reader lane (`screen-reader-lane.md`)** drives real VoiceOver on macOS and NVDA on Windows and asserts that a control’s name, role, and state are spoken together in a single sentence after `"Speech check"` synchronization markers—catching real engine bugs like WebKit `#285047` truncating `<button role="combobox">` speech by three characters, which DOM/ARIA snapshots never see.

3. **Drive native app journeys in ~19 ms instead of ~17 s, and black-box audit every agent door (`Ouro Reins` + `ax-xray`).**
   Today, verifying an iOS or macOS flow via XCUITest or screenshots takes ~15–20 seconds per run and flakes on timing. `OuroReins` exposes each screen’s live focus, state JSON, and narrowed valid action schemas over `ls` and `do` headless with `ReinsNetworkGuard` blocking stray network calls—running Spoonjoy’s kitchen-to-cook-mode journey in **~19 ms versus ~17 s in XCUITest** (and `hackamore` extends the same `ls`/`do` loop to arbitrary Mac apps). Paired with **`ax-xray`**—which probes CLI, HTTP, MCP, and component twins from outside behind fail-closed mock/credential checks, verifies postconditions and receipts, and checks surface inventories (alongside `ax-flows` for multi-step task continuity)—I can run tight, sub-second inner verification loops across both the human and agent sides of an app.

4. **Catch UI misuse in the typechecker before compaction can erase prompt instructions.**
   Instead of relying on a long prompt skill surviving context compaction, Ouro HX encodes accessibility and design invariants directly into TypeScript types (`label`/`title` required, negative prop hint types steering me from `onClick` or `isLoading` to `onOpen` or `loading`), actionable runtime fixes (`[ouro-ui] <Component>: <what's wrong>. Fix: <exact code>`), and deterministic `ouro-census` control-multiset diffs. That lets me catch structural, accessibility, and motion regressions mechanically, and hand human reviewers a build where their time goes only to what `taste-rubric.md` rightly reserves for people: physical spring character, thumb comfort, voice, and taste.
